$$

questions.problem:
Building company policy states that each ton of cement mixture should contain at least $0.7$ tons of sand. What's the minimum amount of sand in $1.2$ tons of cement mixture? Express your answer as a decimal.

There will be a minimum of
{{field-1}}
tons of sand in $1.2$ tons of cement mixture.
questions.worked_solution:
To determine how much sand is in $1.2$ tons of the cement mixture, we have to multiply $1.2$ by $0.7.$

We proceed by multiplying the two numbers just as we would with whole numbers.

Notice that the second number has a leading $0$, which we ignore during the multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\,\,\,\begin{aligned} \\ 1\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.7\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in $1.2$ and there is $1$ decimal place in $0.7.$
Therefore, their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

So, we take our value of $84$ and add a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places.

$$
\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{84}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Hence, $1.2\times 0.7=0.84.$

We conclude that there are $0.84$ tons of sand in $1.2$ tons of the cement mixture.

The building company combines $1.6$ tons of sand with $0.69$ tons of cement to make their cement mixture. What is the total weight of the mixture? Express your answer as a decimal.

The total weight of the mixture is
{{field-1}}
tons.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the total weight of the mixture, we need to calculate the sum $1.6+0.69.$

There is $1$ decimal place in $1.6$ and $2$ decimal places in $0.69.$

To add the numbers, they both need to have the same number of decimals. Hence, we rewrite the first number so that it has $2$ decimal places:

$$
1.6=1.60
$$

Next, we line up the decimal points:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,9\,\,\,\, \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, &  & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by adding the two numbers just as we would with whole numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned} \\ 1\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  &  \\  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,9\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,9\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total weight of the mixture is $2.29$ tons.

questions.problem:
One of the workers cuts $3\,\frac{3}{4}\,\text{ft}$ from a pipe measuring $5\,\frac{1}{8}\,\text{ft}.$ What is the length of the remaining pipe? Express your answer as a mixed number.

The length of the remaining pipe is$\,$
{{field-1}}
$\text{ft}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The length of the remaining pipe is $(5\,\frac{1}{8}-3\,\frac{3}{4})\text{ft}.$

Writing $5\,\frac{1}{8}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
5\,\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5\times 8+1}{8}=\frac{41}{8}.
$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{4}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
3\,\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3\times 4+3}{4}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{15}{4}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $8.$

To put $\frac{15}{4}$ over a denominator of $8,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{15}{4}=\frac{15\times 2}{4\times 2}=\frac{30}{8}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{30}{8}=\frac{11}{8}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{11}{8}=1\,\text{R}\,3=1\,\frac{3}{8}
$$

Therefore, $1\,\frac{3}{8}\,\text{ft}$ of pipe remains.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The length of the remaining pipe is $(5\,\frac{1}{8}-3\,\frac{3}{4})\text{ft}.$

Writing $5\,\frac{1}{8}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
5\,\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5\times 8+1}{8}=\frac{41}{8}.
$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{4}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
3\,\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3\times 4+3}{4}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{15}{4}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $8.$

To put $\frac{15}{4}$ over a denominator of $8,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{15}{4}=\frac{15\times 2}{4\times 2}=\frac{30}{8}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{30}{8}=\frac{11}{8}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{11}{8}=1\,\text{R}\,3=1\,\frac{3}{8}
$$

Therefore, $1\,\frac{3}{8}\,\text{ft}$ of pipe remains.

question.problem:
Building company policy states that each ton of cement mixture should contain at least $0.7$ tons of sand. What's the minimum amount of sand in $1.2$ tons of cement mixture? Express your answer as a decimal.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        There will be a minimum of

tons of sand in $1.2$ tons of cement mixture.
question.worked_solution:
To determine how much sand is in $1.2$ tons of the cement mixture, we have to multiply $1.2$ by $0.7.$

We proceed by multiplying the two numbers just as we would with whole numbers.

Notice that the second number has a leading $0$, which we ignore during the multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\,\,\,\begin{aligned} \\ 1\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.7\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in $1.2$ and there is $1$ decimal place in $0.7.$
Therefore, their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

So, we take our value of $84$ and add a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places.

$$
\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{84}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Hence, $1.2\times 0.7=0.84.$

We conclude that there are $0.84$ tons of sand in $1.2$ tons of the cement mixture.

question.problem:
One of the workers cuts $3\,\frac{3}{4}\,\text{ft}$ from a pipe measuring $5\,\frac{1}{8}\,\text{ft}.$ What is the length of the remaining pipe? Express your answer as a mixed number.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The length of the remaining pipe is$\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\text{ft}.$
question.worked_solution:
The length of the remaining pipe is $(5\,\frac{1}{8}-3\,\frac{3}{4})\text{ft}.$

Writing $5\,\frac{1}{8}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
5\,\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5\times 8+1}{8}=\frac{41}{8}.
$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{4}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
3\,\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3\times 4+3}{4}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{15}{4}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $8.$

To put $\frac{15}{4}$ over a denominator of $8,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{15}{4}=\frac{15\times 2}{4\times 2}=\frac{30}{8}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{30}{8}=\frac{11}{8}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{11}{8}=1\,\text{R}\,3=1\,\frac{3}{8}
$$

Therefore, $1\,\frac{3}{8}\,\text{ft}$ of pipe remains.

question.problem:
The company used $104.7\,\text{ft}$ of piping to construct $5$ identical houses. Estimate the length of piping used for each home by rounding the total piping length to the nearest whole number.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\text{ft}.$
question.worked_solution:
To estimate the length of piping used for each of the $5$ houses, we need to find an approximation for $104.7÷5.$

So, we round the dividend to the nearest whole number:

$$
104.7\to 105
$$

Now, we divide $105$ by $5$ as usual:

$$
105÷5=21
$$

Therefore, the construction of each house used approximately $21\,\text{ft}$ of pipes.

questions.problem: Solve for $a$ where $c=3a+7b.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $a,$ so we will treat the other variables $b$ and $c$ constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $a.$

First, we subtract $7b$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =3a+7b \\ c-7b & =3a+7b-7b \\ c-7b & =3a\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =c-7b \\ \frac{3a}{3} & =\frac{c-7b}{3} \\ a & =\frac{c-7b}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Make $c$ the subject of the equation $-6a=9b-2c.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $c,$ so we will treat the other variables $a$ and $b$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $c.$

First, we add $2c$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a & =9b-2c \\ -6a+2c & =9b-2c+2c \\ -6a+2c & =9b\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $6a$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a+2c & =9b \\ -6a+2c+6a & =9b+6a \\ 2c & =9b+6a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2c & =9b+6a \\ \frac{2c}{2} & =\frac{9b+6a}{2} \\ c & =\frac{9b+6a}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $y=5w+7x,$ then $x=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x,$ so we will treat the other variables $w$ and $y$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $x.$

First, we subtract $5w$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5w+7x \\ y-5w & =5w+7x-5w \\ y-5w & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x & =y-5w \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{y-5w}{7} \\ x & =\frac{y-5w}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Make $k$ the subject of the equation $-2h=2m-3k.$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $k,$ so we will treat the other variables $h$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $k.$

First, we add $3k$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2h & =2m-3k \\ -2h+3k & =2m-3k+3k \\ 3k-2h & =2m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $2h$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3k-2h & =2m \\ 3k-2h+2h & =2m+2h \\ 3k & =2m+2h\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3k & =2m+2h \\ \frac{3k}{3} & =\frac{2m+2h}{3} \\ k & =\frac{2(m+h)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The formula to calculate the distance that an object in uniform rectilinear motion has traveled is given by

$$
d=v\cdot t,
$$

where $v$ represents the velocity of the moving object and $t$ represents time.

What is the formula for velocity in terms of distance and time?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $v,$ so we will treat the other variables $d$ and $t$ as constants. Since $v$ is being multiplied by $t,$ we need to divide both sides of the equation by $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =v\cdot t \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot t}{t} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot \cancel{t}}{\cancel{t}} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $v=\frac{d}{t}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $t\ne 0.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The surface area of a cylinder is given by 

$$
A=2\pi rh
$$

where $r$ is the radius and $h$ is the height of the cylinder.

What is the formula for the height of the cylinder in terms of the other variables?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $h,$ so we will treat the other variables $A$ and $r$ as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by $2\pi r$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2\pi rh \\ A & =(2\pi r)h \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =\frac{(2\pi r)h}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =h\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=\frac{A}{2\pi r}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $r\ne 0.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: If $2xz-3y=4w,$ then $y=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $y,$ so we will treat the other variables $w,x,$ and $z$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $y.$

First, we subtract $2xz$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz-3y & =4w \\ 2xz-3y-2xz & =4w-2xz \\ -3y & =4w-2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-3$ to get $y$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3y & =4w-2xz \\ \frac{-3y}{-3} & =\frac{4w-2xz}{-3} \\ y & =\frac{4w-2xz}{-3} \\ y & =\frac{2xz-4w}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
In business, the economic profit is defined as

$$
E=PQ-C,
$$

where $P$ is the sale price of a good, $Q$ is the number of goods sold, and $C$ is the cost of producing $Q$ goods. 

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $P,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $Q,$ and $C$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $P.$

First, we add $C$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =PQ-C \\ E+C & =PQ-C+C \\ E+C & =PQ\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $Q$ to get $P$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}E+C & =PQ \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =\frac{PQ}{Q} \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $P=\frac{E+C}{Q}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $Q\ne 0.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving Equations When the Variables are Separate
canonical_examples.problem: Solve for $x$ where $2x - y = 5y - z.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x,$ so we will treat the other variables $y$ and $z$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $x.$

First, we add $y$ to both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
		2x - y &= 5y - z \[5pt]
		2x - y + y &= 5y - z + y \[5pt]
		2x &= 6y - z
	}
$$

 

Then, we divide both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2x &= 6y - z \[5pt]
		\dfrac {2x} 2 &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2} \[5pt]
		x &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2}
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving Equations Requiring Manipulation of Binomials
canonical_examples.problem: The total energy $E$ of a body moving with a (squared) velocity $V$ can be approximated using the equation $E = mC + \dfrac{1}{2}mV.$ Find an expression for $V$ in terms of the other quantities.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $V,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $C,$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $V.$

First, we subtract $mC$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =mC+\frac{1}{2}mV \\ E-mC & =mC+\frac{1}{2}mV-mC \\ E-mC & =\frac{1}{2}mV\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we multiply by $2$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}E-mC & =\frac{1}{2}mV \\ 2\cdot (E-mC) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}mV \\ 2(E-mC) & =mV\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide by $m$ to get $V$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(E-mC) & =mV \\ \frac{2(E-mC)}{m} & =\frac{mV}{m} \\ \frac{2(E-mC)}{m} & =V\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $V = \dfrac{2(E-mC)}{m}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $m\neq 0.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes we might be given an equation that contains more than one variable and asked to isolate one of the variables. This means that we need to put the variable we're interested in on one side of the equation (on its own) and everything else on the other.

For example, suppose we want to isolate $n$ in the equation

$$
2n - k = q + 5k.
$$

The equation has three variables, $n,$ $k,$ and $q.$ However, we will treat the variables $k$ and $q$ as constants because we are solving for $n$ only. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $n\mathbin{.}$ 

First, we add $k$ to both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
		2n - k &= q + 5k \[5pt]
		2n - k + k &= q + 5k +k \[5pt]
		2n &= q + 6k \
	}
$$

 

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2n &= q + 6k \[5pt]
		\dfrac {2n} {2} &= \dfrac {q+6k} {2} \
n &= \dfrac {q+6k} {2}
	}
$$

 

Because the equation is now solved for $n$, we say that we've made $n$ **the subject** of the equation.

observed_steps.name: Example: Solving Equations When the Variables are Separate
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x,$ so we will treat the other variables $y$ and $z$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $x.$

First, we add $y$ to both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
		2x - y &= 5y - z \[5pt]
		2x - y + y &= 5y - z + y \[5pt]
		2x &= 6y - z
	}
$$

 

Then, we divide both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2x &= 6y - z \[5pt]
		\dfrac {2x} 2 &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2} \[5pt]
		x &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2}
	}
$$

question.problem: Solve for $x$ where $2x - y = 5y - z.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x,$ so we will treat the other variables $y$ and $z$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $x.$

First, we add $y$ to both sides:

$$
\eqalign{
		2x - y &= 5y - z \[5pt]
		2x - y + y &= 5y - z + y \[5pt]
		2x &= 6y - z
	}
$$

 

Then, we divide both sides by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2x &= 6y - z \[5pt]
		\dfrac {2x} 2 &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2} \[5pt]
		x &= \dfrac{6y - z} {2}
	}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =3a+7b \\ c-7b & =3a+7b-7b \\ c-7b & =3a\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =c-7b \\ \frac{3a}{3} & =\frac{c-7b}{3} \\ a & =\frac{c-7b}{3}\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}-6a+2c & =9b \\ -6a+2c+6a & =9b+6a \\ 2c & =9b+6a\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

Make k the subject of the equation −2h=2m−3k.

a
k=2(h−m)3
b
k=23m−2h
c
k=−m+h2
d
k=2(m+h)3
e
k=m−2h2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate k, so we will treat the other variables h and m as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for k.

First, we add 3k to both sides:

−2h=2m−3k−2h+3k=2m−3k+3k3k−2h=2m Next, we add 2h to both sides: 3k−2h=2m3k−2h+2h=2m+2h3k=2m+2h Then, we divide both sides by 3: 3k=2m+2h3k3=2m+2h3k=2(m+h)3

We need to isolate $V,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $C,$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $V.$

First, we subtract $mC$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =mC+\frac{1}{2}mV \\ E-mC & =mC+\frac{1}{2}mV-mC \\ E-mC & =\frac{1}{2}mV\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we multiply by $2$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}E-mC & =\frac{1}{2}mV \\ 2\cdot (E-mC) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}mV \\ 2(E-mC) & =mV\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide by $m$ to get $V$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(E-mC) & =mV \\ \frac{2(E-mC)}{m} & =\frac{mV}{m} \\ \frac{2(E-mC)}{m} & =V\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $V = \dfrac{2(E-mC)}{m}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $m\neq 0.$

where $P$ is the sale price of a good, $Q$ is the number of goods sold, and $C$ is the cost of producing $Q$ goods. 

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $P,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $Q,$ and $C$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $P.$

First, we add $C$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =PQ-C \\ E+C & =PQ-C+C \\ E+C & =PQ\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $Q$ to get $P$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}E+C & =PQ \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =\frac{PQ}{Q} \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $P=\frac{E+C}{Q}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $Q\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

In business, the economic profit is defined as E=PQ−C,

where P is the sale price of a good, Q is the number of goods sold, and C is the cost of producing Q goods.

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?

a
C=PQ−E
b
P=Q(E+C)
c
P=E+CQ
d
Q=E+CP
e
P=E−CQ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate P, so we will treat the other variables E, Q, and C as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for P.

First, we add C to both sides:

E=PQ−CE+C=PQ−C+CE+C=PQ

Then, we divide by Q to get P alone:

E+C=PQE+CQ=PQQE+CQ=P

Thus, P=E+CQ.

Note: This result assumes that Q≠0.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Solve for $a$ where $c=3a+7b.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $a,$ so we will treat the other variables $b$ and $c$ constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $a.$

First, we subtract $7b$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =3a+7b \\ c-7b & =3a+7b-7b \\ c-7b & =3a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =c-7b \\ \frac{3a}{3} & =\frac{c-7b}{3} \\ a & =\frac{c-7b}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $a,$ so we will treat the other variables $b$ and $c$ constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $a.$

First, we subtract $7b$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =3a+7b \\ c-7b & =3a+7b-7b \\ c-7b & =3a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =c-7b \\ \frac{3a}{3} & =\frac{c-7b}{3} \\ a & =\frac{c-7b}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate a, so we will treat the other variables b and c constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for a.

First, we subtract 7b from both sides:

c=3a+7bc−7b=3a+7b−7bc−7b=3a

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Make $c$ the subject of the equation $-6a=9b-2c.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $c,$ so we will treat the other variables $a$ and $b$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $c.$

First, we add $2c$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a & =9b-2c \\ -6a+2c & =9b-2c+2c \\ -6a+2c & =9b\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $6a$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a+2c & =9b \\ -6a+2c+6a & =9b+6a \\ 2c & =9b+6a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2c & =9b+6a \\ \frac{2c}{2} & =\frac{9b+6a}{2} \\ c & =\frac{9b+6a}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x,$ so we will treat the other variables $w$ and $y$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $x.$

First, we subtract $5w$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5w+7x \\ y-5w & =5w+7x-5w \\ y-5w & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x & =y-5w \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{y-5w}{7} \\ x & =\frac{y-5w}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Make $k$ the subject of the equation $-2h=2m-3k.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $k,$ so we will treat the other variables $h$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $k.$

First, we add $3k$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2h & =2m-3k \\ -2h+3k & =2m-3k+3k \\ 3k-2h & =2m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $2h$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3k-2h & =2m \\ 3k-2h+2h & =2m+2h \\ 3k & =2m+2h\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3k & =2m+2h \\ \frac{3k}{3} & =\frac{2m+2h}{3} \\ k & =\frac{2(m+h)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Make $k$ the subject of the equation $-2h=2m-3k.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $k,$ so we will treat the other variables $h$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $k.$

First, we add $3k$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2h & =2m-3k \\ -2h+3k & =2m-3k+3k \\ 3k-2h & =2m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $2h$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3k-2h & =2m \\ 3k-2h+2h & =2m+2h \\ 3k & =2m+2h\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3k & =2m+2h \\ \frac{3k}{3} & =\frac{2m+2h}{3} \\ k & =\frac{2(m+h)}{3}\end{aligned}

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Make $k$ the subject of the equation $-2h=2m-3k.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $k,$ so we will treat the other variables $h$ and $m$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $k.$

First, we add $3k$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2h & =2m-3k \\ -2h+3k & =2m-3k+3k \\ 3k-2h & =2m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $2h$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3k-2h & =2m \\ 3k-2h+2h & =2m+2h \\ 3k & =2m+2h\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3k & =2m+2h \\ \frac{3k}{3} & =\frac{2m+2h}{3} \\ k & =\frac{2(m+h)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The formula to calculate the distance that an object in uniform rectilinear motion has traveled is given by

$$
d=v\cdot t,
$$

where $v$ represents the velocity of the moving object and $t$ represents time.

What is the formula for velocity in terms of distance and time?
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $v,$ so we will treat the other variables $d$ and $t$ as constants. Since $v$ is being multiplied by $t,$ we need to divide both sides of the equation by $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =v\cdot t \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot t}{t} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot \cancel{t}}{\cancel{t}} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $v=\frac{d}{t}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $t\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The formula to calculate the distance that an object in uniform rectilinear motion has traveled is given by d=v⋅t,

where v represents the velocity of the moving object and t represents time.

What is the formula for velocity in terms of distance and time?

a
v=d⋅t
b
v=dt
c
v=tv
d
v=d−t
e
v=d+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate v, so we will treat the other variables d and t as constants. Since v is being multiplied by t, we need to divide both sides of the equation by t:

d=v⋅tdt=v⋅ttdt=v⋅ttdt=v

Thus, v=dt.

Note: This result assumes that t≠0.

last_observation.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =v\cdot t \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot t}{t} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =\frac{v\cdot \cancel{t}}{\cancel{t}} \\ \frac{d}{t} & =v\end{aligned}

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

The formula to calculate the distance that an object in uniform rectilinear motion has traveled is given by d=v⋅t,

where v represents the velocity of the moving object and t represents time.

What is the formula for velocity in terms of distance and time?

a
v=d⋅t
b
v=dt
c
v=tv
d
v=d−t
e
v=d+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate v, so we will treat the other variables d and t as constants. Since v is being multiplied by t, we need to divide both sides of the equation by t:

d=v⋅tdt=v⋅ttdt=v⋅ttdt=v

Thus, v=dt.

Note: This result assumes that t≠0.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The surface area of a cylinder is given by 

$$
A=2\pi rh
$$

where $r$ is the radius and $h$ is the height of the cylinder.

What is the formula for the height of the cylinder in terms of the other variables?
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $h,$ so we will treat the other variables $A$ and $r$ as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by $2\pi r$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2\pi rh \\ A & =(2\pi r)h \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =\frac{(2\pi r)h}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =h\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=\frac{A}{2\pi r}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $r\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The surface area of a cylinder is given by A=2πrh where r is the radius and h is the height of the cylinder.

What is the formula for the height of the cylinder in terms of the other variables?

a
h=A2π
b
h=12Aπr
c
h=2Aπr
d
h=Aπr
e
h=A2πr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate h, so we will treat the other variables A and r as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by 2πr

A=2πrhA=(2πr)hA2πr=(2πr)h2πrA2πr=h

Therefore, h=A2πr.

Note: This result assumes that r≠0.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $h,$ so we will treat the other variables $A$ and $r$ as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by $2\pi r$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2\pi rh \\ A & =(2\pi r)h \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =\frac{(2\pi r)h}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{A}{2\pi r} & =h\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=\frac{A}{2\pi r}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $r\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The surface area of a cylinder is given by A=2πrh where r is the radius and h is the height of the cylinder.

What is the formula for the height of the cylinder in terms of the other variables?

a
h=A2π
b
h=12Aπr
c
h=2Aπr
d
h=Aπr
e
h=A2πr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate h, so we will treat the other variables A and r as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by 2πr

A=2πrhA=(2πr)hA2πr=(2πr)h2πrA2πr=h

Therefore, h=A2πr.

Note: This result assumes that r≠0.

What is the formula for the height of the cylinder in terms of the other variables?

h=Aπr
e
h=A2πr
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate h, so we will treat the other variables A and r as constants.

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by 2πr

A=2πrhA=(2πr)hA2πr=(2πr)h2πrA2πr=h

Therefore, h=A2πr.

question.problem: If $2xz-3y=4w,$ then $y=${{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $y,$ so we will treat the other variables $w,x,$ and $z$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $y.$

First, we subtract $2xz$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz-3y & =4w \\ 2xz-3y-2xz & =4w-2xz \\ -3y & =4w-2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-3$ to get $y$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3y & =4w-2xz \\ \frac{-3y}{-3} & =\frac{4w-2xz}{-3} \\ y & =\frac{4w-2xz}{-3} \\ y & =\frac{2xz-4w}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
In business, the economic profit is defined as

$$
E=PQ-C,
$$

where $P$ is the sale price of a good, $Q$ is the number of goods sold, and $C$ is the cost of producing $Q$ goods. 

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?
question.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $P,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $Q,$ and $C$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $P.$

First, we add $C$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =PQ-C \\ E+C & =PQ-C+C \\ E+C & =PQ\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $Q$ to get $P$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}E+C & =PQ \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =\frac{PQ}{Q} \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $P=\frac{E+C}{Q}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $Q\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

In business, the economic profit is defined as E=PQ−C,

where P is the sale price of a good, Q is the number of goods sold, and C is the cost of producing Q goods.

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?

a
C=PQ−E
b
P=Q(E+C)
c
P=E+CQ
d
Q=E+CP
e
P=E−CQ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate P, so we will treat the other variables E, Q, and C as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for P.

First, we add C to both sides:

E=PQ−CE+C=PQ−C+CE+C=PQ

Then, we divide by Q to get P alone:

E+C=PQE+CQ=PQQE+CQ=P

Thus, P=E+CQ.

Note: This result assumes that Q≠0.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $P,$ so we will treat the other variables $E,$ $Q,$ and $C$ as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for $P.$

First, we add $C$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =PQ-C \\ E+C & =PQ-C+C \\ E+C & =PQ\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $Q$ to get $P$ alone:

$$
\begin{aligned}E+C & =PQ \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =\frac{PQ}{Q} \\ \frac{E+C}{Q} & =P\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $P=\frac{E+C}{Q}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $Q\ne 0.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

In business, the economic profit is defined as E=PQ−C,

where P is the sale price of a good, Q is the number of goods sold, and C is the cost of producing Q goods.

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?

a
C=PQ−E
b
P=Q(E+C)
c
P=E+CQ
d
Q=E+CP
e
P=E−CQ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate P, so we will treat the other variables E, Q, and C as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for P.

First, we add C to both sides:

E=PQ−CE+C=PQ−C+CE+C=PQ

Then, we divide by Q to get P alone:

E+C=PQE+CQ=PQQE+CQ=P

Thus, P=E+CQ.

Note: This result assumes that Q≠0.

solution.reasoning: Add C to both sides to get E+C=PQ, then divide by Q, assuming Q\neq 0. Thus P=\frac{E+C}{Q}, choice c. No captured answer or grade establishes Math Academy's key for this question.

feedback.html:
Question 8
?

In business, the economic profit is defined as E=PQ−C,

where P is the sale price of a good, Q is the number of goods sold, and C is the cost of producing Q goods.

What is the formula for the price in terms of the other variables?

a
C=PQ−E
b
P=Q(E+C)
c
P=E+CQ
d
Q=E+CP
e
P=E−CQ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to isolate P, so we will treat the other variables E, Q, and C as constants. We can use the addition and multiplication principles to solve for P.

First, we add C to both sides:

E=PQ−CE+C=PQ−C+CE+C=PQ

Then, we divide by Q to get P alone:

E+C=PQE+CQ=PQQE+CQ=P

Thus, P=E+CQ.

Note: This result assumes that Q≠0.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 19\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}19 & -7 \\ -7 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
4.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[13−1],w=[2−21],x=[4−2−8].

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
questions.raw_html:
5.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

E
Tue, Oct 13th @ 4:09 AM|Elapsed: 0:32Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 19\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}19 & -7 \\ -7 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[111],w=[313],x=[345].

a
[2−42]
b
[−42−4]
c
[333]
d
[444]
e
[543]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[131113]⟹AT=[111313].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[131113]⋅([111313]⋅[131113])−1⋅[111313]⋅[345]=[131113]⋅[37719]−1⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅18[19−7−73]⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅[40]=[444]

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we verify whether a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors a1 and a2 that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[1−11221]⇒AT=[112−121].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[1−11221]⋅([112−121]⋅[1−11221])−1⋅[112−121]⋅[363]=[1−11221]⋅[6336]−1⋅[1512]=[1−11221]⋅19[2−1−12]⋅[1512]=[1−11221]⋅[21]=[145]

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Verify whether the vectors a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the vectors {a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[212],a2=[1−11],a3=[−1−2−1],x=[301].

a
[454]
b
[202]
c
[222]
d
[313]
e
[151]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we verify whether a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[21−11−1−221−1]R3:=R3−R1M=[21−11−1−2000]R2↔R1∼[1−1−221−100−0]R2:=R2−2R1∼[1−1−2033000]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors a1 and a2 that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[211−121]⇒AT=[2121−11].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[211−121]⋅([2121−11]⋅[211−121])−1⋅[2121−11]⋅[301]=[211−121]⋅[9333]−1⋅[84]=[211−121]⋅16[1−1−13]⋅[84]=13[211−121]⋅[22]=[202]

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$

$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[13−1],w=[2−21],x=[4−2−8].

a
[−3−10]
b
[103]
c
[310]
d
[1−30]
e
[013]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[123−2−11]⟹AT=[13−12−21].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[123−2−11]⋅([13−12−21]⋅[123−2−11])−1⋅[13−12−21]⋅[4−2−8]=[123−2−11]⋅[11−5−59]−1⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅174[95511]⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅[11]=[310]

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[1−2−3]
b
[−31−3]
c
[3−2−1]
d
[32−3]
e
[12−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[3101−11]⟹AT=[30−1111].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[3101−11]⋅([30−1111]⋅[3101−11])−1⋅[30−1111]⋅[2−60]=[3101−11]⋅[10223]−1⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅126[3−2−210]⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅[1−2]=[1−2−3]

judgments.reasoning: The plane consists of vectors with equal first and third coordinates, so the projection of (3,4,5) is (4,4,4). Its residual (−1,0,1) is perpendicular to both spanning vectors. This agrees with my earlier answer and Math Academy’s worked solution. The recorded submission was option a, (2,−4,2), rather than my recommended option d; its Incorrect grade is mathematically consistent.

The vectors are dependent because a₁=a₂+a₃. Their span is the plane z=x+y, with normal (−1,−1,1). Removing the normal component of (3,6,3) gives (1,4,5)=2a₁+a₂. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted option b graded Correct, and Math Academy’s worked solution.

The vectors are dependent because a₁−a₂+a₃=0. Their span is the plane with equal first and third coordinates, so projecting (3,0,1) gives (2,0,2). The residual (1,0,−1) is perpendicular to the span. This agrees with my earlier option b and Math Academy’s worked solution. The actual submission was option a, (4,5,4), so its Incorrect grade is consistent.
A normal is n=v×w=(1,−3,−8). Since x·n=n·n=74, the projection is x−n=(3,1,0)=v+w. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted option c graded Correct, and Math Academy’s worked solution.

The closest vector is p=a₁−2a₂=(1,−2,−3). The residual x−p=(1,−4,3) has zero dot product with both a₁ and a₂, proving p is the orthogonal projection. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted option a graded Correct, and Math Academy’s worked solution.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 7 \\ 7 & 19\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}19 & -7 \\ -7 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ 28\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[111],w=[313],x=[345].

a

b
[−42−4]

[333]

EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[131113]⟹AT=[111313].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[131113]⋅([111313]⋅[131113])−1⋅[111313]⋅[345]=[131113]⋅[37719]−1⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅18[19−7−73]⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅[40]=[444]

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$

$$

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[111],w=[313],x=[345].

a
[2−42]
b

EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[131113]⟹AT=[111313].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[131113]⋅([111313]⋅[131113])−1⋅[111313]⋅[345]=[131113]⋅[37719]−1⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅18[19−7−73]⋅[1228]=[131113]⋅[40]=[444]

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}15 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Verify whether the vectors a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the vectors {a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[112],a2=[−121],a3=[2−11],x=[363].

a
[−154]
b
[145]
c
[033]
d
[2−11]
e
[178]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we verify whether a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[1−1212−1211]R2:=R2−R1R3:=R3−2R1∼[1−1203−303−3]R3:=R3−R2∼[1−1203−3000]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors a1 and a2 that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[1−11221]⇒AT=[112−121].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[1−11221]⋅([112−121]⋅[1−11221])−1⋅[112−121]⋅[363]=[1−11221]⋅[6336]−1⋅[1512]=[1−11221]⋅19[2−1−12]⋅[1512]=[1−11221]⋅[21]=[145]

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Verify whether the vectors a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the vectors {a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[212],a2=[1−11],a3=[−1−2−1],x=[301].

a
[454]
b
[202]
c
[222]
d
[313]
e
[151]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we verify whether a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[21−11−1−221−1]R3:=R3−R1M=[21−11−1−2000]R2↔R1∼[1−1−221−100−0]R2:=R2−2R1∼[1−1−2033000]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors a1 and a2 that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[211−121]⇒AT=[2121−11].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[211−121]⋅([2121−11]⋅[211−121])−1⋅[2121−11]⋅[301]=[211−121]⋅[9333]−1⋅[84]=[211−121]⋅16[1−1−13]⋅[84]=13[211−121]⋅[22]=[202]
