last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Verify whether the vectors a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the vectors {a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[212],a2=[1−11],a3=[−1−2−1],x=[301].

EXPLANATION

First, we verify whether a1,a2,a3 are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[21−11−1−221−1]R3:=R3−R1M=[21−11−1−2000]R2↔R1∼[1−1−221−100−0]R2:=R2−2R1∼[1−1−2033000]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors a1 and a2 that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[211−121]⇒AT=[2121−11].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[211−121]⋅([2121−11]⋅[211−121])−1⋅[2121−11]⋅[301]=[211−121]⋅[9333]−1⋅[84]=[211−121]⋅16[1−1−13]⋅[84]=13[211−121]⋅[22]=[202]

solution.reasoning: The vectors are linearly dependent because a₁−a₂+a₃=0. The independent vectors a₁ and a₂ span the plane whose first and third coordinates are equal. Projecting x=(3,0,1) onto this plane averages those coordinates, giving (2,0,2). The residual (1,0,−1) is perpendicular to every spanning vector. feedback.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 4
?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[13−1],w=[2−21],x=[4−2−8].

a
[−3−10]
b
[103]
c
[310]
d
[1−30]
e
[013]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[123−2−11]⟹AT=[13−12−21].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[123−2−11]⋅([13−12−21]⋅[123−2−11])−1⋅[13−12−21]⋅[4−2−8]=[123−2−11]⋅[11−5−59]−1⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅174[95511]⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅[11]=[310]

solution.reasoning: A normal to the plane is n=v×w=(1,−3,−8). Since x·n=74 and n·n=74, the projection is x−((x·n)/(n·n))n=(4,−2,−8)−(1,−3,−8)=(3,1,0). This also equals v+w, so it lies in the plane. Option c is mathematically correct; no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{74}[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[13−1],w=[2−21],x=[4−2−8].

a
[−3−10]
b
[103]
c
[310]
d
[1−30]
e
[013]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[123−2−11]⟹AT=[13−12−21].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[123−2−11]⋅([13−12−21]⋅[123−2−11])−1⋅[13−12−21]⋅[4−2−8]=[123−2−11]⋅[11−5−59]−1⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅174[95511]⋅[64]=[123−2−11]⋅[11]=[310]

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[1−2−3]
b
[−31−3]
c
[3−2−1]
d
[32−3]
e
[12−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[3101−11]⟹AT=[30−1111].

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[1−2−3]
b
[−31−3]
c
[3−2−1]
d
[32−3]
e
[12−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[3101−11]⟹AT=[30−1111].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[3101−11]⋅([30−1111]⋅[3101−11])−1⋅[30−1111]⋅[2−60]=[3101−11]⋅[10223]−1⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅126[3−2−210]⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅[1−2]=[1−2−3]

solution.reasoning: The closest vector is the orthogonal projection. A normal to the subspace is n=a₁×a₂=(1,−4,3). Since x·n=n·n=26, the projection is x−n=(1,−2,−3), which equals a₁−2a₂ and therefore lies in the subspace. Its residual is perpendicular to the subspace, establishing that option a is correct. feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[1−2−3]
b
[−31−3]
c
[3−2−1]
d
[32−3]
e
[12−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[3101−11]⟹AT=[30−1111].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[3101−11]⋅([30−1111]⋅[3101−11])−1⋅[30−1111]⋅[2−60]=[3101−11]⋅[10223]−1⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅126[3−2−210]⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅[1−2]=[1−2−3]

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14164468/assets/663096ab9ecc1daca22587d94526cbf0db841602ca0b64eaa1a9477ec8a35aee.png)

What is the length of $a$ in the triangle shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we know the lengths of the hypotenuse and one leg, so let $b=12$ and $c=13.$ We need to find $a,$ the length of the other leg.

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & ={c}^{2}-{b}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $b$ and $c$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\sqrt{(13)^{2}-(12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{169-144} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the length of $a$ in the triangle shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we know the lengths of the hypotenuse and one leg, so let $b=\frac{15}{2}$ and $c=\frac{39}{2}.$ We need to find $a,$ the length of the other leg.

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & ={c}^{2}-{b}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $b$ and $c$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\sqrt{{(\frac{39}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{15}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\,521}{4}-\frac{225}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{324} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: A right triangle has legs of length $4$ and $8.$ Calculate the length of its hypotenuse.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $a=4,$ $b=8,$ and $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $a$ and $b$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}+(8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we know the lengths of the hypotenuse and one leg, so let $b=12$ and $c=13.$ We need to find $a,$ the length of the other leg.

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & ={c}^{2}-{b}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $b$ and $c$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\sqrt{(13)^{2}-(12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{169-144} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

A right triangle has legs of length 4 and 8. Calculate the length of its hypotenuse.

a
10
b
45
c
210
d
72
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let a=4, b=8, and c be the length of the hypotenuse. According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain c2=a2+b2c=a2+b2.

Substituting in the values for a and b gives us c=(4)2+(8)2=16+64=80=45.

What is the length of $a$ in the triangle shown above?
question.worked_solution:
Here, we know the lengths of the hypotenuse and one leg, so let $b=12$ and $c=13.$ We need to find $a,$ the length of the other leg.

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & ={c}^{2}-{b}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $b$ and $c$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\sqrt{(13)^{2}-(12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{169-144} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: A right triangle has legs of length $4$ and $8.$ Calculate the length of its hypotenuse.
question.worked_solution:
Let $a=4,$ $b=8,$ and $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in the values for $a$ and $b$ gives us

$$

a
10
b
45
c
210
d

e
12
Submit
Correct

Let a=4, b=8, and c be the length of the hypotenuse. According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain c2=a2+b2c=a2+b2.

Substituting in the values for a and b gives us c=(4)2+(8)2=16+64=80=45.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $3{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/52d095f73fdaa91c6a2fe9f2caca74929a22ec09618e85395732ea451bda81c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $3{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =-(2)^{3}+C \\ C & =2+8 \\ C & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=10-{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10-{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =10-{x}^{3} \\ {x}^{3} & =10 \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{10}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/4b08d915d0adf8bf603070aa96bde1edf0cfb392d9be5f9bd4786897a6c943fa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+1 \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=9-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $4x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\sqrt{2}\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=2\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =2(2\sqrt{2})^{2}+C \\ C & =6-16 \\ C & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}-10.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2} & =5 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{5}\,m\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(2x-3)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $3\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/ca6267f534b9cad9bc1646eef473d85aab1ba6a5f4738b8212b107b753ea2381.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x-3)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x-3.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x-3.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x-3)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-3x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=3\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(3)^{2}-3(3)+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-3x+2.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-3x+2 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =1\,m,\,2\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(3+kx)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=8\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/f368d2de12462a1790322edca188232bf8fafe3951facdb29b334e285807b9fe.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3+kx)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3+kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3+kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (3+kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =3(0)+\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+32.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x+\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+32 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8\sqrt{2})^{2} & =3(8)+\frac{k(8)^{2}}{2}+32 \\ 64 & =24+32k+32 \\ 32k & =8 \\ k & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m$ and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\pi \,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/b396b80995e34fe348b3d059737b1eec3d4ce5a9d2e9138a8e7d4ed5c0945dc0.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=\pi \,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\ 32 & =8+k \\ k & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $k{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=8\sqrt{17}\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has a velocity of $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $4\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/f3879ccc6084d9a0ef8bef2e211e2e7fd9dcc811fb04f06c2ef7429e4d574871.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $k{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-k{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-k{x}^{3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-k{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=8\sqrt{17}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8\sqrt{17})^{2} & =-\frac{k}{4}(0)^{4}+C \\ C & =544\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=544-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4}.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=4\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =544-\frac{k}{4}{x}^{4} \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =544-\frac{k}{4}(4)^{4} \\ 32 & =544-64k \\ 64k & =512 \\ k & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\sqrt[3]{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/771929267e75b5d45b9777399c784fafc570386834eee6738fead9ff1bb78e5e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\sqrt[3]{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\sqrt[3]{x}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\sqrt[3]{x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}(0)^{4/3}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+2.
$$

Finally, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}{x}^{4/3}+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =\frac{3k}{4}(8)^{4/3}+2 \\ 32 & =12k+2 \\ 12k & =30 \\ k & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=20\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $10\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=20\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(20)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =200\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=10\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}(10)^{2} \\ 50k & =200 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/33b95a6985a53b76eb7f74771825c18f21d1e59b2245325e14690a365a2a8bb0.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=10-2x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10-2x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=5\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $4$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=5\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=10-2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (10-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=10x-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =10(0)-(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(5)=\sqrt{-2(5)^{2}+20(5)+4}=3\sqrt{6}\,m/s
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(8-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/5a1fa0d49dc7a35d176473d3554de6383fa042cc2c5daf7eb5abaad1d5b387cd.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(8-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(8-2x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(8-2x) & =0 \\ 8-2x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $3$ |  | $5$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2k>0$ | $0$ | $-2k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(8-2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(8-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(8x-{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(8x-{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(8(0)-(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(8x-{x}^{2})+3.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(8x-{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{5})^{2} & =k(8(1)-{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 10 & =7k+3 \\ 7k & =7 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(8x-{x}^{2})+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =16x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+16x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+16x+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-2(4)^{2}+16(4)+6}=\sqrt{38}\,m/s
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/51ccc6e3e341931c7a244c4617ede78f901478487589f9023b16c3dae80ebc62.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=7-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=7-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (7-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =7(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =14x-{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(7)=\sqrt{-(7)^{2}+14(7)+6}=\sqrt{55}\,m/s
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(6-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/a8ff5e02237554d0f7107168f287adbe1834c4dd7ad965163531f5a23412a4fc.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(6-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(6-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(6-x) & =0 \\ 6-x & =0 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=6\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,6)$ | $6$ | $(6,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $5$ |  | $7$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=6\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(6-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(6-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(6(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{11})^{2} & =k(6(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+2 \\ 22 & =10k+2 \\ 10k & =20 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =12x-{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =24x-2{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(6)=\sqrt{-2(6)^{2}+24(6)+4}=2\sqrt{19}\,m/s
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/0f8f7773a5e55c81de553eccf684f9a6128dd6e76e06b9040d5953371e72184f.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=3\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $4$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=3\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (3-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =6x-{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(3)=\sqrt{6(3)-(3)^{2}+4}=\sqrt{13}\,m/s.
$$

15.?

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x where x≥0. When the displacement of P from the origin is xm, the velocity is vm/s, and the acceleration is (3−x)m/s2. If P has velocity v=2m/s at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest
canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x \geq 1.$  When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(2x-2) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $\sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1\,\rm{m},$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/0c47a1e988a75e4813c92a76acbf3a821364995123f3eb394b07d4bfaa95f80d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x \geq 1$ is $x=2\,\rm{m}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding an Unknown Value
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ the velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and the acceleration is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \,\rm{m},$ find the value of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/6280c4b1561cda0d16c6758bb5d8fae30d66d9925bd1bb9db1a29e70093c6f61.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2 kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2kx \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + 2.
$$

Finally, since $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(1)^{2}+2 \\ 8 & =k+2 \\ k & =6\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Unknown Value

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Maximum Speed of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x \geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x \, \rm{m},$ the velocity is $v \, \rm{m/s},$ and the acceleration is $k(5 - x) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v = \sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ at the origin and has velocity $v = 2\sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \, \rm{m},$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/c129b3157bf3741f4e1fa30c7bb97eaa0bff11ff1eef1e2ee548f2653a4da7d2.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(5 - x)\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = k(5 - x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(5-x) & =0 \\ 5-x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x = 5 \, \rm{m}.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,5)$ | $5$ | $(5,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $4$ |  | $6$ |
| $\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}$ | $k > 0$ | $0$ | $-k <         0$ |
| $v$ | $\color{red}\nearrow$ | max | $\color{blue}\searrow$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x = 5\,\rm{m}.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = k(5 - x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int k(5 - x) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = k\left(5x - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) + C.
$$

Now, since $v = \sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 0 \, \rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = k\left(5x - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) + 3.
$$

Also, since $v = 2\sqrt{6} \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 1 \, \rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(1)-\frac{1}{2}{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 12 & =\frac{9k}{2}+3 \\ \frac{9k}{2} & =9 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \sqrt{-2x^2 + 20x + 6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\max} = v(5) =\sqrt{-2(5)^2 + 20(5) + 6} = 2\sqrt{14}\,\rm{m/s}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Maximum Speed of a Particle

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.  

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$ 

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int 2x \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when $P$ is instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\,m\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.content:
We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.  

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$ 

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int 2x \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when $P$ is instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\,m\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}

\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+1 \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=9-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =9-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin is x meters, its velocity is vm/s, the magnitude of its acceleration is 2xm/s2, and the acceleration is directed toward O. If P has velocity 4m/s when its displacement is 1m, find the values of x for which P is instantaneously at rest.

a
x=±52m
b
x=2m
c
x=4m
d
x=±1m
e
x=±3m
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P has magnitude 2xm/s2 and is directed toward O, we have

dvdt=−2x.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=−2x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have

∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(−2x)dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=−x2+C.

Now, since v=4m/s when x=1m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows:

12v2=−x2+C12(4)2=−(1)2+CC=8+1C=9

Therefore,

12v2=9−x2.

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when v(x)=0m/s. We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting v=0 in the equation above and solving for x:

12v2=9−x212(0)2=9−x2x2=9x=±3m.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=2\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =2(2\sqrt{2})^{2}+C \\ C & =6-16 \\ C & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}-10.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =2{x}^{2}-10 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2} & =5 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{5}\,m\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P moves along the x-axis. When the displacement of P from the origin is xm, the velocity is vm/s, and the acceleration is 4xm/s2. If P has velocity 23m/s when its displacement is 22m, find the values of x for which P is instantaneously at rest.

a
x=±2m
b
x=±32m
c
x=3m
d
x=5m
e
x=±5m

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 4xm/s2, we have

dvdt=4x.

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=4x.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have

∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫4xdx

which gives the general solution

12v2=2x2+C.

Now, since v=23m/s when x=22m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows:

12v2=2x2+C12(23)2=2(22)2+CC=6−16C=−10

Therefore,

12v2=2x2−10.

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when v(x)=0m/s. We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting v=0 in the equation above and solving for x:

12v2=2x2−1012(0)2=2x2−102x2=10x2=5x=±5m

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

question.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

Question 4
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x≥12. When the displacement of P from the origin is x meters, its velocity is vm/s, the magnitude of its acceleration is (4x−2)m/s2, and the acceleration is directed toward O. If P has velocity 1m/s when its displacement is 12m, find the value of x for which P is instantaneously at rest.

a
x=3m
b
x=3m
c
x=1m
d
x=32m
e
x=2m
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P has magnitude (4x−2)m/s2 and is directed toward O, we have

dvdt=−(4x−2).

Using the fact that dvdt=ddx(12v2), we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=−(4x−2).

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have

∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫(−4x+2)dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=−2x2+2x+C.

Now, since v=1m/s when x=12m, we can find the value of the constant C, as follows:

12v2=−2x2+2x+C12(1)2=−2(12)2+2(12)+CC=12+12−1C=0

Therefore,

12v2=−2x2+2x.

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when v(x)=0m/s. We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting v=0 in the equation above and solving for x:

12v2=−2x2+2x12(0)2=−2x2+2x2x(1−x)=0.

The only solution of this equation for x≥12 is x=1m.
