Question 11
?

∫−1/1202x+16x+1dx=

a
116(3+ln⁡3)
b
136(1+4ln⁡2)
c
136(1+2ln⁡3)
d
116(1+5ln⁡2)
e
125(5+ln⁡5)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we pull out the factor of 6 from the denominator: ∫−1/1202x+16x+1dx=∫−1/1202x+16(x+16)dx=16∫−1/1202x+1(x+16)dx.

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder. xx0−1621↓−13223

So from the synthetic division, we get that 2x+1(x+16)=2+(23)(x+16)=2+46x+1.

Therefore, ∫−1/1202x+16x+1dx=16∫−1/120(2+46x+1)dx=16[2∫−1/120dx+4∫−1/12016x+1dx]=16[2x+46ln⁡|6x+1|]−1/120=16[2x+23ln⁡|6x+1|]−1/120=16[2(0−(−112))+23(ln⁡|6(0)+1|−ln⁡|6(−112)+1|)]=16[2(112)+23(ln⁡1−ln⁡(12))]=16[16+23ln⁡2]=136(1+4ln⁡2).
question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient

solution.reasoning: The integrand decomposes as 1/3+(2/3)/(6x+1), with antiderivative x/3+(1/9)\ln|6x+1|. Evaluating from -1/12 to 0 gives 1/36+(1/9)\ln 2=(1+4\ln 2)/36, matching option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $6$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6(x+\frac{1}{6})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{6})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{6} & 2 & 1 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{1}{3} \\  & 2 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+1}{(x+\frac{1}{6})} & =2+\frac{(\frac{2}{3})}{(x+\frac{1}{6})} \\  & =2+\frac{4}{6x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{2x+1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}(2+\frac{4}{6x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-1/12}^{0}\frac{1}{6x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[2x+\frac{4}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+1|]}_{-1/12}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[2x+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|6x+1|]}_{-1/12}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2(0-(-\frac{1}{12}))+\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|6(0)+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|6(-\frac{1}{12})+1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[2(\frac{1}{12})+\frac{2}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\frac{1}{6}+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2] \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(1+4\operatorname{ln}⁡2).\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Evaluate the following integral:

${\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}} $-\,\frac{13}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-2}} $)$
question.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{3}$ | $7$ | $-2$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-\frac{7}{3}$ |
|  | $7$ | $-\frac{13}{3}$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7x-2}{(x+1/3)} & =7-\frac{(13/3)}{(x+1/3)} \\  & =7-\frac{13}{3x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{7x-2}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(7-\frac{13}{3x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[7{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}x-13{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[7x-\frac{13}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[7(1-0)-\frac{13}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[7-\frac{13\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3}] \\  & =\frac{7}{3}-\frac{13}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4).\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Evaluate the following integral:

${\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-4}{4x+3}\,\text{d}x=$ 
{{field-1}} $-\,\frac{31}{16}\operatorname{ln}⁡($

question.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-4}{4x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-4}{4(x+\frac{3}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{3}{4}$ | $5$ | $-4$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-\frac{15}{4}$ |
|  | $5$ | $-\frac{31}{4}$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{4})} & =5-\frac{(\frac{31}{4})}{(x+\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =5-\frac{31}{4x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-4}{4x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}(5-\frac{31}{4x+3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[5{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-31{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[5x-\frac{31}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x+3|]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[5(2-0)-\frac{31}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|11|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[10-\frac{31}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{11}{3})] \\  & =\frac{5}{2}-\frac{31}{16}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{11}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4x-5}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4x-5}{3(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4x-5}{(x+1/3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{3}$ | $4$ | $-5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-\frac{4}{3}$ |
|  | $4$ | $-\frac{19}{3}$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x-5}{(x+1/3)} & =4-\frac{(19/3)}{(x+1/3)} \\  & =4-\frac{19}{3x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{4x-5}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-\frac{19}{3x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[4{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-19{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[4x-\frac{19}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[4(2-0)-\frac{19}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|7|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[8-\frac{19\operatorname{ln}⁡7}{3}] \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{19}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(7).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}-9{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}42 \\ -70\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{4}\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{12}{9\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 3+0\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}})≈{23.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[34−8],{x1+2x2−2x3=03x1+6x2−6x3=0

H
Tue, Oct 13th @ 4:28 AM|Elapsed: 0:15Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[121],a2=[212],x=[321].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
34.05∘
b
22.21∘
c
14.21∘
d
45.12∘
e
54.05∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[122112]⟹AT=[121212].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[122112]⋅([121212]⋅[122112])−1⋅[121212]⋅[321]=[122112]⋅[6669]−1⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[12−13−1313]⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[2323]=[222].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=3⋅2+2⋅2+1⋅232+22+12⋅22+22+22=121412=12242=642

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(642)≈22.21∘,

which is already an acute angle.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}42 \\ -70\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}-9{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

Question 2
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−81−8],{3x1−6x2−9x3=0−2x1+4x2+6x3=0

a
[−93−5]
b
[561]
c
[−63−1]
d
[−95−6]
e
[−11−5]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[3−6−90−2460]R1:=13R1∼[1−2−30−2460]R2:=R2+2R1∼[1−2−300000]

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=2x2+3x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x2+3x3x2x3]=x2[210]+x3[301],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[210],[301]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[231001]⋅([210301]⋅[231001])−1⋅[210301]⋅[−81−8]=[231001]⋅[56610]−1⋅[−15−32]=[231001]⋅114[10−6−65]⋅[−15−32]=[231001]⋅114[42−70]=[231001]⋅[3−5]=[−93−5]

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{4}\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{12}{9\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[220],a2=[−11−1],x=[5−52].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
17.36∘
b
18.88∘
c
21.83∘
d
20.02∘
e
19.47∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[2−1210−1]⟹AT=[220−11−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[2−1210−1]⋅([220−11−1]⋅[2−1210−1])−1⋅[220−11−1]⋅[5−52]=[2−1210−1]⋅[8003]−1⋅[0−12]=[2−1210−1]⋅[180013]⋅[0−12]=[2−1210−1]⋅[0−4]=4[1−11].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx. Equivalently, it is the acute angle between x and any non-zero vector that is parallel to projSx. So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

x=[5−52] and 14projSx=[1−11].

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=5⋅1+(−5)⋅(−1)+2⋅152+(−5)2+22⋅12+(−1)2+12=12543=1292=432

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(432)≈19.47∘,

which is already an acute angle.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 3+0\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}})≈{23.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Question 4
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[212],a2=[−10−1],x=[−230].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
20.77∘
b
21.99∘
c
23.09∘
d
19.17∘
e
22.85∘
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[2−1102−1]⟹AT=[212−10−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[2−1102−1]⋅([212−10−1]⋅[2−1102−1])−1⋅[212−10−1]⋅[−230]=[2−1102−1]⋅[9−4−42]−1⋅[−12]=[2−1102−1]⋅[12292]⋅[−12]=[2−1102−1]⋅[37]=[−13−1].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=(−2)⋅(−1)+3⋅3+0⋅(−1)(−2)2+32+02⋅(−1)2+32+(−1)2=111311=1113

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(1113)≈23.09∘,

which is already an acute angle.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=−2x2+2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [−2x2+2x3x2x3]=x2[−210]+x3[201],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[−210],[201]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[121],a2=[212],x=[321].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
34.05∘
b
22.21∘
c
14.21∘
d
45.12∘
e
54.05∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[122112]⟹AT=[121212].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[122112]⋅([121212]⋅[122112])−1⋅[121212]⋅[321]=[122112]⋅[6669]−1⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[12−13−1313]⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[2323]=[222].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=3⋅2+2⋅2+1⋅232+22+12⋅22+22+22=121412=12242=642

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(642)≈22.21∘,

which is already an acute angle.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Question 1
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[121],a2=[212],x=[321].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
34.05∘
b
22.21∘
c
14.21∘
d
45.12∘
e
54.05∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[122112]⟹AT=[121212].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[122112]⋅([121212]⋅[122112])−1⋅[121212]⋅[321]=[122112]⋅[6669]−1⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[12−13−1313]⋅[810]=[122112]⋅[2323]=[222].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=3⋅2+2⋅2+1⋅232+22+12⋅22+22+22=121412=12242=642

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(642)≈22.21∘,

which is already an acute angle.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}-9{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-15 \\ -32\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}42 \\ -70\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−81−8],{3x1−6x2−9x3=0−2x1+4x2+6x3=0

a
[−93−5]
b
[561]
c
[−63−1]
d
[−95−6]
e
[−11−5]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[3−6−90−2460]R1:=13R1∼[1−2−30−2460]R2:=R2+2R1∼[1−2−300000]

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=2x2+3x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x2+3x3x2x3]=x2[210]+x3[301],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[210],[301]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[231001]⋅([210301]⋅[231001])−1⋅[210301]⋅[−81−8]=[231001]⋅[56610]−1⋅[−15−32]=[231001]⋅114[10−6−65]⋅[−15−32]=[231001]⋅114[42−70]=[231001]⋅[3−5]=[−93−5]

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 1 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}-9{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & -9 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

$$

question.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{4}\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{12}{9\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{4}\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{12}{9\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Question 3

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[220],a2=[−11−1],x=[5−52].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
17.36∘
b
18.88∘
c
21.83∘
d
20.02∘
e
19.47∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[2−1210−1]⟹AT=[220−11−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[2−1210−1]⋅([220−11−1]⋅[2−1210−1])−1⋅[220−11−1]⋅[5−52]=[2−1210−1]⋅[8003]−1⋅[0−12]=[2−1210−1]⋅[180013]⋅[0−12]=[2−1210−1]⋅[0−4]=4[1−11].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx. Equivalently, it is the acute angle between x and any non-zero vector that is parallel to projSx. So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

x=[5−52] and 14projSx=[1−11].

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=5⋅1+(−5)⋅(−1)+2⋅152+(−5)2+22⋅12+(−1)2+12=12543=1292=432

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(432)≈19.47∘,

which is already an acute angle.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 3+0\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}})≈{23.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 3+0\cdot (-1)}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{13}\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{13}})≈{23.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[212],a2=[−10−1],x=[−230].

Round the answer to 2 decimal places.

a
20.77∘
b
21.99∘
c
23.09∘
d
19.17∘
e
22.85∘
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[2−1102−1]⟹AT=[212−10−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[2−1102−1]⋅([212−10−1]⋅[2−1102−1])−1⋅[212−10−1]⋅[−230]=[2−1102−1]⋅[9−4−42]−1⋅[−12]=[2−1102−1]⋅[12292]⋅[−12]=[2−1102−1]⋅[37]=[−13−1].

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=(−2)⋅(−1)+3⋅3+0⋅(−1)(−2)2+32+02⋅(−1)2+32+(−1)2=111311=1113

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(1113)≈23.09∘,

which is already an acute angle.

solution.reasoning: Both spanning vectors satisfy v_1=v_3, so their plane has normal n=(1,0,-1). The acute angle θ between x and the plane satisfies sin θ=|x·n|/(||x||||n||)=2/(\sqrt{13}\sqrt{2})=2/\sqrt{26}. Thus θ≈23.09347°, which rounds to 23.09°, option c. question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{x}^{2}-4y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3-5x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=1$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2}-4y)={x}^{2}-4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x)={x}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-5x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={x}^{3}y-x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x{y}^{3}-y$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{x+y}-2y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{x+y}-2x$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-3$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}y-x)={x}^{3} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{3}-y)={y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}-2y)={e}^{x+y}-2 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}-2x)={e}^{x+y}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x-1})=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x{e}^{xy}$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2y+1$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2y+1$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+1)=2 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only'.

$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}=\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{yz}\cdot (\frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{yz}}{(x+y)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot ({e}^{yz}+yz{e}^{yz}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =-\frac{{e}^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2}-4y)={x}^{2}-4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-4x)={x}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-5x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-2{y}^{3}{e}^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{yz}\cdot (\frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{yz}}{(x+y)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot ({e}^{yz}+yz{e}^{yz}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =-\frac{{e}^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that a function f(x,y,z) and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set U, and that

∂2f∂y2=xeyzx+y,∂2f∂x∂z=−zeyzx+y.

Evaluate the following expression at the point (1,1,0):

∂3f∂y∂x∂y+∂3f∂z∂x∂z

a
−12
b
−14
c
34
d
32
e
43
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set U, the mixed partial derivatives must be equal.

Hence, we have

∂3f∂y∂x∂y=∂3f∂x∂y2=∂∂x(∂2f∂y2)=∂∂x(xeyzx+y)=eyz⋅(1⋅(x+y)−x⋅1(x+y)2)=yeyz(x+y)2.

In addition, we have ∂3f∂z∂x∂z=∂∂z(∂2f∂x∂z)=∂∂z(−zeyzx+y)=−1x+y⋅(eyz+yzeyz)=−eyz(1+yz)x+y.

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point (1,1,0):

∂3f∂x∂y∂x|(1,1,0)=1⋅e1⋅0(1+1)2=14∂3f∂z∂x∂z|(1,1,0)=−e1⋅0(1+1⋅0)1+1=−12

Finally, we get

∂3f∂x∂y∂x|(1,1,0)+∂3f∂z∂x∂z|(1,1,0)=14−12=−14.
