question.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨0,e3x,2y⟩ and the scalar field f(x,y,z)=2x+3. Given that ∇×F=⟨2,0,3e3x⟩,∇f=⟨2,0,0⟩, calculate ∇×(fF) at the point (0,−1,4).

a
⟨0,−1,4⟩
b
⟨−3,0,1⟩
c
⟨9,3,4⟩
d
⟨0,4,1⟩
e
⟨6,4,11⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We shall use the following identity: ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F

First, we compute ∇f×F. We get ∇f×F=|ijk2000e3x2y|=[0(2y)−0(e3x)]i−[2(2y)−0(0)]j+[2(e3x)−0(0)]k=0i−4yj+2e3xk=⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩.

Therefore, we have ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F=(2x+3)⟨2,0,3e3x⟩+⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩=⟨2(2x+3),0,(6x+9)e3x⟩+⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩=⟨2(2x+3),−4y,(6x+11)e3x⟩.

Finally, ∇×(fF)(0,−1,4)=⟨2(2(0)+3),−4(−1),(6(0)+11)e3(0)⟩=⟨6,4,11⟩.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{3x} & 2y\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(2y)-0({e}^{3x})]i-[2(2y)-0(0)]j+[2({e}^{3x})-0(0)]k \\  & =0\,i-4y\,j+2{e}^{3x}\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(2x+3)⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),0,(6x+9){e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),-4y,(6x+11){e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,4) & =⟨2(2(0)+3),-4(-1),(6(0)+11){e}^{3(0)}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,4,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
∇\times F=⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩,\,∇f=⟨2,0,0⟩,

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,4).$

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨0,e3x,2y⟩ and the scalar field f(x,y,z)=2x+3. Given that ∇×F=⟨2,0,3e3x⟩,∇f=⟨2,0,0⟩, calculate ∇×(fF) at the point (0,−1,4).

a
⟨0,−1,4⟩
b
⟨−3,0,1⟩
c
⟨9,3,4⟩
d
⟨0,4,1⟩
e
⟨6,4,11⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We shall use the following identity: ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F

First, we compute ∇f×F. We get ∇f×F=|ijk2000e3x2y|=[0(2y)−0(e3x)]i−[2(2y)−0(0)]j+[2(e3x)−0(0)]k=0i−4yj+2e3xk=⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩.

Therefore, we have ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F=(2x+3)⟨2,0,3e3x⟩+⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩=⟨2(2x+3),0,(6x+9)e3x⟩+⟨0,−4y,2e3x⟩=⟨2(2x+3),−4y,(6x+11)e3x⟩.

Finally, ∇×(fF)(0,−1,4)=⟨2(2(0)+3),−4(−1),(6(0)+11)e3(0)⟩=⟨6,4,11⟩.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,{e}^{3x},2y⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=2x+3.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩,\,∇f=⟨2,0,0⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,4).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{3x} & 2y\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(2y)-0({e}^{3x})]i-[2(2y)-0(0)]j+[2({e}^{3x})-0(0)]k \\  & =0\,i-4y\,j+2{e}^{3x}\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(2x+3)⟨2,0,3{e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),0,(6x+9){e}^{3x}⟩+⟨0,-4y,2{e}^{3x}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(2x+3),-4y,(6x+11){e}^{3x}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,4) & =⟨2(2(0)+3),-4(-1),(6(0)+11){e}^{3(0)}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,4,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\sqrt{x},0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=-z.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,0,-1⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(4,1,4).$
question.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ z & \sqrt{x} & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(0)-(-1)(\sqrt{x})]i-[0(0)-(-1)(z)]j+[0(\sqrt{x})-0(z)]k \\  & =\sqrt{x}\,i-z\,j+0\,k \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(-z)⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-2z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(4,1,4) & =⟨\sqrt{4},-2(4),-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-8,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨z,x,0⟩ and the scalar field f(x,y,z)=−z. Given that ∇×F=⟨0,1,12x⟩,∇f=⟨0,0,−1⟩, calculate ∇×(fF) at the point (4,1,4).

a
⟨1,4,0⟩
b
⟨−2,4,0⟩
c
⟨−4,1,1⟩
d
⟨−4,−1,−4⟩
e
⟨2,−8,−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We shall use the following identity: ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F

First, we compute ∇f×F. We get

∇f×F=|ijk00−1zx0|=[0(0)−(−1)(x)]i−[0(0)−(−1)(z)]j+[0(x)−0(z)]k=xi−zj+0k=⟨x,−z,0⟩.

Therefore, we have ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F=(−z)⟨0,1,12x⟩+⟨x,−z,0⟩=⟨0,−z,−z2x⟩+⟨x,−z,0⟩=⟨x,−2z,−z2x⟩.

Finally, ∇×(fF)(4,1,4)=⟨4,−2(4),−424⟩=⟨2,−8,−1⟩.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ z & \sqrt{x} & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(0)-(-1)(\sqrt{x})]i-[0(0)-(-1)(z)]j+[0(\sqrt{x})-0(z)]k \\  & =\sqrt{x}\,i-z\,j+0\,k \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(-z)⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-2z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(4,1,4) & =⟨\sqrt{4},-2(4),-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-8,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\sqrt{x},0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=-z.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,0,-1⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(4,1,4).$
question.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(-z)⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-2z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(4,1,4) & =⟨\sqrt{4},-2(4),-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-8,-1⟩.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 10
?

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨z,x,0⟩ and the scalar field f(x,y,z)=−z. Given that ∇×F=⟨0,1,12x⟩,∇f=⟨0,0,−1⟩, calculate ∇×(fF) at the point (4,1,4).

a
⟨1,4,0⟩
b
⟨−2,4,0⟩
c
⟨−4,1,1⟩
d
⟨−4,−1,−4⟩
e
⟨2,−8,−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We shall use the following identity: ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F

First, we compute ∇f×F. We get

∇f×F=|ijk00−1zx0|=[0(0)−(−1)(x)]i−[0(0)−(−1)(z)]j+[0(x)−0(z)]k=xi−zj+0k=⟨x,−z,0⟩.

Therefore, we have ∇×(fF)=f∇×F+∇f×F=(−z)⟨0,1,12x⟩+⟨x,−z,0⟩=⟨0,−z,−z2x⟩+⟨x,−z,0⟩=⟨x,−2z,−z2x⟩.

Finally, ∇×(fF)(4,1,4)=⟨4,−2(4),−424⟩=⟨2,−8,−1⟩.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\sqrt{x},0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=-z.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,0,-1⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(4,1,4).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ z & \sqrt{x} & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =[0(0)-(-1)(\sqrt{x})]i-[0(0)-(-1)(z)]j+[0(\sqrt{x})-0(z)]k \\  & =\sqrt{x}\,i-z\,j+0\,k \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(-z)⟨0,1,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩+⟨\sqrt{x},-z,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{x},-2z,-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{x}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(4,1,4) & =⟨\sqrt{4},-2(4),-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-8,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Convert $\frac{17}{8}$ into a decimal using long division.
questions.worked_solution:
To write down the given fraction as a decimal, we need to divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 17÷8 $$ We proceed using the long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0:$
$\,\,\,2\,.\,1\,2\,5$
$8$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{1\,\phantom{|}7\,.\,0\,\phantom{|}0\,\phantom{|}0}$
$-\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $1$ $6$
$1$ $0$
$-\,\,\,\,\,$ $8$
$2$ $0$
$-\,\,\,\,\,$ $1$ $6$
$4$ $0$
$-\,\,\,\,\,$ $4$ $0$
$0$

Therefore, $$ \frac{17}{8}=2.125. $$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Convert $\frac{35}{6}$ into a repeating decimal using long division.
questions.worked_solution:
To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 35÷6 $$ We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:


$\,\,\,5\,.\,8\,3\,3\,…$
$6$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{3\,\phantom{|}5\,.\,0\,\phantom{|}0\,\phantom{|}0}$
$-\,\,\,\,\,\,$$3$ $0$
$5$ $0$
$-\,\,\,$ $4$ $8$
$2$ $0$
$-$$1$ $8$
$2$ $\,0$
$-\,\,$ $1$ $\,8$
$\,2$
$\,⋮$

We could continue the division, but the same digit keeps repeating. Thus, the decimal continues with repeating $3$'s: $$ 5.833… $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{35}{6}=5.833…=5.8\overset{―}{3}. $$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $1.353124…$

II. $1.5\overset{―}{21}$

III. $4.055$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.353124…$ is not a rational number. The notation "$…$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. However, there are no repeating digits.

- $1.5\overset{―}{21}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overset{―}{21}$ tells us that the digits $2$ and $1$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=1.52121212121…
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=\frac{1\,506}{990}.
$$

- $4.055$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
4.055=\frac{4\,055}{1\,000}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $3.624$

II. $0.\overset{―}{25}$

III. $7.526380…$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $3.624$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
3.624=\frac{3\,624}{1\,000}
$$

- $0.\overset{―}{25}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overset{―}{25}$ tells us that the digits $2$ and $5$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
0.\overset{―}{25}=0.2525252525…
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
0.\overset{―}{25}=\frac{25}{99}.
$$

- $7.526380…$ is not a rational number. The notation "$…$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. However, there are no repeating digits.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical_examples.problem: Convert $\dfrac{35}{4}$ into a decimal using long division.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator:

$$
35 \div 4
$$

We proceed using long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0$:

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{35}{4} = 8.75.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Rational Number as a Finite Decimal Using Long Division

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing a Rational Number as a Repeating Decimal Using Long Division
canonical_examples.problem: Convert $\dfrac{79}{6}$ into a repeated decimal using long division.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator:

$$
79 \div 6
$$

We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152429/assets/3c9add129b16a1dedeb68e0397f6345d7f481f3bbfdd54c0a35067abaaa15263.svg)

We could continue the division, but the same digit keeps repeating. Thus, the decimal continues with repeating $6$'s:

$$
13.16\ldots
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{79}{6} = 13.16\ldots = 13.1\overline{6}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Rational Number as a Repeating Decimal Using Long Division

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Rational Decimals
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $1.577$

II. $8.163452 \ldots$

III. $2.\overline{73}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.577$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
1.577 = \dfrac{1\,577}{1\,000}
$$

- $8.163452 \ldots$ is not a rational number. The notation "$\ldots$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. Because there is no indicated repeating pattern, this represents a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal.

- $2.\overline{73}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overline{73}$ tells us that the digits $7$ and $3$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
2.\overline{73} = 2.73737373\ldots
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
2.\overline{73}  = \dfrac{271}{99}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A rational number can have a decimal representation that either *ends* or *repeats*. In this lesson, we will see how to convert rational numbers written as fractions into decimals using *long division*. We begin with examples where the decimal terminates. Let's convert $\dfrac{7}{2}$ into a decimal using long division. To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 7 \div 2 $$ We proceed using long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0\mathbin{:}$
$\,\,3 {\, . \,} 5$
$2$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{7 {\, . \,} 0}$
$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $6$
$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $1$ $0$
$0$

Therefore, $$ \dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5. $$

tutorials.name: Repeating Decimals
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the following rational number: $$ \dfrac13 $$ To find its decimal representation, we divide $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:
$\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3$ $\:\ldots$
$3$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\, . \,} 0 {\:\phantom{|}} 0 {\:\phantom{|}} 0}$
$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $\,\ldots$

Notice that, in this case, - the long division process never ends, and - the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*. Therefore, $$ \dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ This is an example of a **repeating decimal** - a decimal in which the digits after the decimal point continue forever in a *repeating pattern*.

tutorials.name: Notations for Repeating Decimals
tutorials.problem:
It's convenient to use the following special **bar-notation** to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely:

$$
0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.\overset{―}{78} & =0.78\,78\,78\,78… \\ 0.\overset{―}{675} & =0.675\,675\,675…\end{aligned}
$$

Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example:

$$
0.45\overline{67} = 0.45\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots
$$

tutorials.name: Any Repeating Decimal is a Rational
tutorials.problem:
The key takeaway for this lesson is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.\overset{―}{3} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ 0.\overset{―}{78} & =\frac{26}{33} \\ 0.333\overset{―}{67} & =\frac{16517}{49500}\end{aligned}
$$

In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. For now, you can verify these results using a calculator.

tutorial.problem:
A rational number can have a decimal representation that either *ends* or *repeats*. In this lesson, we will see how to convert rational numbers written as fractions into decimals using *long division*. We begin with examples where the decimal terminates. Let's convert $\dfrac{7}{2}$ into a decimal using long division. To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 7 \div 2 $$ We proceed using long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of $0\mathbin{:}$

$0$

Therefore, $$ \dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5. $$

tutorial.name: Repeating Decimals
tutorial.problem:
Let's consider the following rational number: $$ \dfrac13 $$ To find its decimal representation, we divide $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:
$\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3$ $\:\ldots$
$3$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\, . \,} 0 {\:\phantom{|}} 0 {\:\phantom{|}} 0}$
$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $\,\ldots$

Notice that, in this case, - the long division process never ends, and - the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*. Therefore, $$ \dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ This is an example of a **repeating decimal** - a decimal in which the digits after the decimal point continue forever in a *repeating pattern*.

Let's consider the following rational number: $$ \dfrac13 $$ To find its decimal representation, we divide $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:
$\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3 {\:\phantom{|}} 3$ $\:\ldots$

$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$

$1$ $0$
$-\!\!\!\!\!$ $9$
$1$ $\,\ldots$

Notice that, in this case, - the long division process never ends, and - the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*. Therefore, $$ \dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ This is an example of a **repeating decimal** - a decimal in which the digits after the decimal point continue forever in a *repeating pattern*.

tutorial.name: Any Repeating Decimal is a Rational
tutorial.problem:
The key takeaway for this lesson is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.\overset{―}{3} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ 0.\overset{―}{78} & =\frac{26}{33} \\ 0.333\overset{―}{67} & =\frac{16517}{49500}\end{aligned}
$$

In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. For now, you can verify these results using a calculator.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Rational Number as a Repeating Decimal Using Long Division
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 35÷6 $$ We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:


$\,\,\,5\,.\,8\,3\,3\,…$
$6$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{3\,\phantom{|}5\,.\,0\,\phantom{|}0\,\phantom{|}0}$
$-\,\,\,\,\,\,$$3$ $0$
$5$ $0$
$-\,\,\,$ $4$ $8$
$2$ $0$
$-$$1$ $8$
$2$ $\,0$
$-\,\,$ $1$ $\,8$
$\,2$
$\,⋮$

We could continue the division, but the same digit keeps repeating. Thus, the decimal continues with repeating $3$'s: $$ 5.833… $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{35}{6}=5.833…=5.8\overset{―}{3}. $$

Question 5
?

Convert 356 into a repeating decimal using long division.

a
5.63―
b
5.76―
c
5.83―
d
5.38―
e
5.66―
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: 35÷6

We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:



0|5.8|3|3…
6 3|5.0|0|0
−3 0
5 0
− 4 8
2 0
−1 8
2 0
− 1 8
2
⋮

We could continue the division, but the same digit keeps repeating. Thus, the decimal continues with repeating 3's: 5.833…

Therefore, 356=5.833…=5.83―.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Rational Number as a Repeating Decimal Using Long Division
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.577$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
1.577 = \dfrac{1\,577}{1\,000}
$$

- $8.163452 \ldots$ is not a rational number. The notation "$\ldots$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. Because there is no indicated repeating pattern, this represents a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal.

- $2.\overline{73}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overline{73}$ tells us that the digits $7$ and $3$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
2.\overline{73} = 2.73737373\ldots
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
2.\overline{73}  = \dfrac{271}{99}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Question 1
?

Convert 178 into a decimal using long division.

a
3.125
b
2.175
c
2.125
d
2.135
e
2.215
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To write down the given fraction as a decimal, we need to divide the numerator by the denominator: 17÷8

We proceed using the long division as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of 0:

0|2.1|2|5
8 1|7.0|0|0
− 1 6
1 0
− 8
2 0
− 1 6
4 0
− 4 0
0

Therefore, 178=2.125.

question.problem: Convert $\frac{35}{6}$ into a repeating decimal using long division.
question.worked_solution:
To write the fraction as a decimal, we divide the numerator by the denominator: $$ 35÷6 $$ We proceed using long division as usual, continuing until a repeating pattern of digits appears after the decimal point:


$\,\,\,5\,.\,8\,3\,3\,…$
$6$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{3\,\phantom{|}5\,.\,0\,\phantom{|}0\,\phantom{|}0}$
$-\,\,\,\,\,\,$$3$ $0$
$5$ $0$
$-\,\,\,$ $4$ $8$
$2$ $0$
$-$$1$ $8$
$2$ $\,0$
$-\,\,$ $1$ $\,8$
$\,2$
$\,⋮$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are rational?

I. $1.353124…$

II. $1.5\overset{―}{21}$

III. $4.055$
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of our numbers in turn.

- $1.353124…$ is not a rational number. The notation "$…$" tells us that digits after the decimal point extend forever. However, there are no repeating digits.

- $1.5\overset{―}{21}$ is a rational number. The notation $\overset{―}{21}$ tells us that the digits $2$ and $1$ after the decimal point repeat indefinitely.

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=1.52121212121…
$$

Any decimal with repeating digits can be represented as a ratio of two integers. In this case,

$$
1.5\overset{―}{21}=\frac{1\,506}{990}.
$$

- $4.055$ is a rational number because it can be expressed as a ratio of two integers:

$$
4.055=\frac{4\,055}{1\,000}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the two numbers in the table that $0.2900$ lies between. These numbers are $0.2877$ and $0.2912.$ So, we have the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.2877 & <0.2900<0.2912\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above inequality in terms of $Φ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.56) & <Φ(z)<Φ(-0.55).\end{aligned}
$$

So, using interval bisection, we can approximate $z$ as

$$
z≈\frac{-0.56+(-0.55)}{2}=-0.555.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The table below gives the values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of $z$ such that $P(Z\le z)=0.40.$ Use the table below and do not round your answer.

| $\,p\,$ | $0.10$ | $0.15$ | $0.20$ | $0.25$ | $0.30$ | $0.35$ | $0.40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ | $\,-0.5244\,$ | $\,-0.3853\,$ | $\,-0.2533\,$ |

$z=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le z) & =0.40 \\ Φ(z) & =0.40\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.40).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.40,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.40\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=-0.2533.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.40)=-0.2533.
$$

Therefore, the required value of $z$ is $-1.2816.$

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.75).
$$

$$
p=0.75\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=0.6745.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.75)=0.6745.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the two numbers in the table that $0.1450$ lies between. These numbers are $0.1446$ and $0.1469.$ So, we have the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.1446 & <0.1450<0.1469\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above inequality in terms of $\Phi,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.06) & <Φ(z)<Φ(-1.05).\end{aligned}
$$

So, using interval bisection, we can approximate $z$ as

$$
z \approx \dfrac{-1.06 + (-1.05)}{2} = -1.055.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When working with normally distributed random variables, we often want to find a value of $z$ that gives rise to a specific probability. 

For example, suppose that $Z\sim N(0,1),$ and we wish to find the value of $z$ such that

$$
P(Z\leq z) = 0.85.
$$

Therefore, our problem is to find a value of $z$ such that $\Phi(z) = 0.85.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14165008/assets/dc2006ce351b075c735f9fc1ace31d5688cd39639a6c526810011b44e631be44.png)

A good place to start is the CDF table for $\Phi(z)$ around the $z$-values where $\Phi(z)\approx 0.85.$ This part of the table is shown below.

| $z$ | $\, 0.03 \,$ | $\, 0.04 \,$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 1.0 \,$ | $\, 0.8485 \,$ | $\, 0.8508 \,$ | $\, 0.8531 \,$ |
| $\, 1.1 \,$ | $\, 0.8708 \,$ | $\, 0.8729 \,$ | $\, 0.8749 \,$ |
| $\, 1.2 \,$ | $\, 0.8907 \,$ | $\, 0.8925 \,$ | $\, 0.8944 \,$ |

There is no listed value of $z$ where $\Phi(z) = 0.85$ exactly. However, notice that there are values where $\Phi(z)$ is slightly below and slightly above $0.85{:}$

- $\Phi(1.03) = 0.8485 < 0.85$

- $\Phi(1.04) = 0.8508 > 0.85$

Therefore, the required value of $z$ must lie between $1.03$ and $1.04.$ To approximate this value of $z,$ we take the average of these two numbers:

$$
z = \dfrac{1.03 + 1.04}{2} = 1.035
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\Phi(1.035) \approx 0.85.
$$

Taking the average of two numbers on an interval to find an improved approximation is known as **interval bisection**.

Taking the average of two numbers on an interval to find an improved approximation is known as **interval bisection**.
tutorial.content:
When working with normally distributed random variables, we often want to find a value of $z$ that gives rise to a specific probability. 

For example, suppose that $Z\sim N(0,1),$ and we wish to find the value of $z$ such that

$$
P(Z\leq z) = 0.85.
$$

Therefore, our problem is to find a value of $z$ such that $\Phi(z) = 0.85.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14165008/assets/dc2006ce351b075c735f9fc1ace31d5688cd39639a6c526810011b44e631be44.png)

A good place to start is the CDF table for $\Phi(z)$ around the $z$-values where $\Phi(z)\approx 0.85.$ This part of the table is shown below.

| $z$ | $\, 0.03 \,$ | $\, 0.04 \,$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 1.0 \,$ | $\, 0.8485 \,$ | $\, 0.8508 \,$ | $\, 0.8531 \,$ |
| $\, 1.1 \,$ | $\, 0.8708 \,$ | $\, 0.8729 \,$ | $\, 0.8749 \,$ |
| $\, 1.2 \,$ | $\, 0.8907 \,$ | $\, 0.8925 \,$ | $\, 0.8944 \,$ |

There is no listed value of $z$ where $\Phi(z) = 0.85$ exactly. However, notice that there are values where $\Phi(z)$ is slightly below and slightly above $0.85{:}$

- $\Phi(1.03) = 0.8485 < 0.85$

- $\Phi(1.04) = 0.8508 > 0.85$

Therefore, the required value of $z$ must lie between $1.03$ and $1.04.$ To approximate this value of $z,$ we take the average of these two numbers:

$$
z = \dfrac{1.03 + 1.04}{2} = 1.035
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\Phi(1.035) \approx 0.85.
$$

Taking the average of two numbers on an interval to find an improved approximation is known as **interval bisection**.

tutorial.name: Using a Percentage Table To Find the Z-Score for a Given Probability
tutorial.problem:
One final way to find the $z$-score for a given probability is to simply look it up in a **percentage points table**, such as the one below.

| $\quad p \quad$ | $0.55$ | $0.60$ | $0.65$ | $0.70$ | $0.75$ | $0.80$ | $0.85$ | $0.90$ | $0.95$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.1257\,$ | $\,0.2533\,$ | $\,0.3853\,$ | $\,0.5244\,$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ |

This table gives the values of $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p = \Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

Let's use the table above to find $z$ such that $P(Z \leq z) = 0.75.$
First, we express the given information in terms of $\Phi{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le z) & =0.75 \\ Φ(z) & =0.75\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z = \Phi^{-1}(0.75).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.75,$ and we find that

$$
p = 0.75 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Phi^{-1}(p) = 0.6745.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z = \Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6745.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.56) & <Φ(z)<Φ(-0.55).\end{aligned}

$$
z≈\frac{-0.56+(-0.55)}{2}=-0.555.
$$

question.problem:

| $\,p\,$ | $0.10$ | $0.15$ | $0.20$ | $0.25$ | $0.30$ | $0.35$ | $0.40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ | $\,-0.5244\,$ | $\,-0.3853\,$ | $\,-0.2533\,$ |

$z=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le z) & =0.40 \\ Φ(z) & =0.40\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.40).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.40,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.40\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=-0.2533.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.40)=-0.2533.
$$

Question 8
?

The table below gives the values of Φ−1(p) for different values of p, where p=Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of z such that P(Z≤z)=0.995.

p 0.900 0.950 0.975 0.990 0.995 0.999 0.9995
Φ−1(p) 1.2816 1.6449 1.9600 2.3263 2.5758 3.0902 3.2905
a
3.2905
b
1.9600
c
1.6449
d
2.3263
e
2.5758
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express the given information in terms of Φ:

P(Z≤z)=0.995Φ(z)=0.995

So, we are looking for the value of z such that

z=Φ−1(0.995).

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to p=0.995, and we find that

p=0.995⇒Φ−1(p)=2.5758.

Therefore, we have

z=Φ−1(0.995)=2.5758.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ,$ using the complement:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>z) & =0.01 \\ 1-P(Z\le z) & =0.01 \\ 1-Φ(z) & =0.01 \\ Φ(z) & =1-0.01 \\ Φ(z) & =0.99\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.99).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.99,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.99\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=2.3263.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.99)=2.3263.
$$

p 0.900 0.950 0.975 0.990 0.995 0.999 0.9995
Φ−1(p) 1.2816 1.6449 1.9600 2.3263 2.5758 3.0902 3.2905
a
−2.3263
b
1.2816
c
−1.2816
d
3.0902
e
2.3263
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express the given information in terms of Φ, using the complement:

P(Z>z)=0.011−P(Z≤z)=0.011−Φ(z)=0.01Φ(z)=1−0.01Φ(z)=0.99

So, we are looking for the value of z such that

z=Φ−1(0.99).

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to p=0.99, and we find that

p=0.99⇒Φ−1(p)=2.3263.

Therefore, we have

z=Φ−1(0.99)=2.3263.

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
From the table, notice that

$$
P(Z\le 1.2816)=0.90.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
P(Z\ge 1.2816)=1-0.90=0.10.
$$

By the symmetry of the standard normal distribution, we have

$$
Φ(-1.2816)=0.10.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14165008/assets/feb06180815c7ae83a5034ff8933700fd5778c9ab0bfba54fe95bb67104662b7.png)

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.2816) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le -1.2816) & =0.10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required value of $z$ is $-1.2816.$

$$
Φ(-1.2816)=0.10.

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.2816) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le -1.2816) & =0.10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required value of $z$ is $-1.2816.$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of $z$ such that $P(Z>z)=0.25.$ Use the table below and do not round your answer.

| $\,p\,$ | $0.65$ | $0.70$ | $0.75$ | $0.80$ | $0.85$ | $0.90$ | $0.95$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.3853\,$ | $\,0.5244\,$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ |

$z=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ,$ using the complement:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>z) & =0.25 \\ 1-P(Z\le z) & =0.25 \\ 1-Φ(z) & =0.25 \\ Φ(z) & =1-0.25 \\ Φ(z) & =0.75\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.75).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.75,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.75\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=0.6745.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.75)=0.6745.
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The table below gives the values of Φ−1(p) for different values of p, where p=Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of z such that P(Z≤z)=0.015.

p 0.965 0.970 0.975 0.980 0.985 0.990 0.995
Φ−1(p) 1.8119 1.8808 1.9600 2.0537 2.1701 2.3263 2.5758
a
−1.9600
b
−1.6449
c
−2.1701
d
1.8808
e
2.5758
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the table, notice that

P(Z≤2.1701)=0.985.

Therefore, we have

P(Z≥2.1701)=1−0.985=0.015.

By the symmetry of the standard normal distribution, we have

Φ(−2.1701)=0.015.

Therefore, we conclude that

Φ(−2.1701)=0.015P(Z≤−2.1701)=0.015.

Therefore, the required value of z is −2.1701.

$$
P(Z\le 2.1701)=0.985.

$$
P(Z\ge 2.1701)=1-0.985=0.015.

$$
Φ(-2.1701)=0.015.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
questions.raw_html:
1.Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function?

Let f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2+z2. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4).

H
Tue, Oct 13th @ 4:50 AM|Elapsed: 0:21Correct

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,3)=-9,\,{f}_{x}(x,y,z)=y,\,{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=x,\,{f}_{z}(x,y,z)=-2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3),$ estimate the value of $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,3)+∇f(1,0,3)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,3),{f}_{y}(1,0,3),{f}_{z}(1,0,3)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,0,3)$, ${f}_{y}(1,0,3)$ and ${f}_{z}(1,0,3),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,0,3) & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(1,0,3) & =1 \\ {f}_{z}(1,0,3) & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.98,y=-0.01$ and $z=3.1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.98,-0.01,3.1) & ≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨0.98-1,-0.01,3.1-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨-0.02,-0.01,0.1⟩ \\  & =-9-0.01-0.6 \\  & =-9.61\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-1.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,0,-1)=1,\,{f}_{x}(1,0,-1)=-1,\,{f}_{y}(1,0,-1)=-1,\,{f}_{z}(1,0,-1)=0.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,-1)$ estimate the value of $f(1.02,0.1,-0.96)$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,-1)+∇f(1,0,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-(-1)⟩ \\  & =f(1,0,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,-1),{f}_{y}(1,0,-1),{f}_{z}(1,0,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z+1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.02,0.1,-0.96)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02,$ $y=0.1,$ and $z=-0.96$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.02,0.1,-0.96) & ≈1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1.02-1,0.1,-0.96+1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,0.1,0.04⟩ \\  & =1-1(0.02)-1(0.1)+0(0.04) \\  & =1-0.02-0.1+0 \\  & =0.88\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2+z2. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4).

a
f(x,y,z)≈13−x54−y54−z54
b
f(x,y,z)≈13−x108−y54−z54
c
f(x,y,z)≈13+x108+y54+z54
d
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108+y54+z54
e
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108−y108−z108
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4) is f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(2,4,4)=16. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fx(2,4,4)=−2(22+42+42)3/2=−1108,fy=−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fy(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154,fz=−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fz(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (2,4,4) is given by ∇f(2,4,4)=⟨fx(2,4,4),fy(2,4,4),fz(2,4,4)⟩=⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16+⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16−1108(x−2)−154(y−4)−154(z−4)=16−x108+154−y54+454−z54+454=13−x108−y54−z54.

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$

$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,3)+∇f(1,0,3)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,3),{f}_{y}(1,0,3),{f}_{z}(1,0,3)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,0,3)$, ${f}_{y}(1,0,3)$ and ${f}_{z}(1,0,3),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,0,3) & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(1,0,3) & =1 \\ {f}_{z}(1,0,3) & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.98,y=-0.01$ and $z=3.1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.98,-0.01,3.1) & ≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨0.98-1,-0.01,3.1-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨-0.02,-0.01,0.1⟩ \\  & =-9-0.01-0.6 \\  & =-9.61\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$

$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Let f(x,y)=xy2−1. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3).

a
f(x,y)≈23−9x−6y
b
f(x,y)≈23+9x−6y
c
f(x,y)≈41+6x+12y
d
f(x,y)≈35+9x+12y
e
f(x,y)≈35−9x+6y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3) is f(x,y)≈f(−2,−3)+∇f(−2,−3)⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−2,−3)=−19. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=y2⇒fx(−2,−3)=(−3)2=9,fy=2xy⇒fy(−2,−3)=2(−2)(−3)=12.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−2,−3) is given by ∇f(−2,−3)=⟨9,12⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y)≈f(−2,−3)+∇f(−2,−3)⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩=−19+⟨9,12⟩⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩=−19+9(x+2)+12(y+3)=35+9x+12y.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Let f(x,y)=xey. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2).

a
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2−x−y
b
f(x,y)≈−2−x+y
c
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x−2y
d
f(x,y)≈−2+2x−2y
e
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x+y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−1,ln⁡2)=−2. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=ey⇒fx(−1,ln⁡2)=eln⁡2=2,fy=xey⇒fy(−1,ln⁡2)=−1eln⁡2=−2.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is given by ∇f(−1,ln⁡2)=⟨2,−2⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+⟨2,−2⟩⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+2(x+1)−2(y−ln⁡2)=2ln⁡2+2x−2y.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,-1)+∇f(1,0,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-(-1)⟩ \\  & =f(1,0,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,-1),{f}_{y}(1,0,-1),{f}_{z}(1,0,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z+1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(1.02,0.1,-0.96)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02,$ $y=0.1,$ and $z=-0.96$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.02,0.1,-0.96) & ≈1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1.02-1,0.1,-0.96+1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨-1,-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,0.1,0.04⟩ \\  & =1-1(0.02)-1(0.1)+0(0.04) \\  & =1-0.02-0.1+0 \\  & =0.88\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2+z2. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4).

a
f(x,y,z)≈13−x54−y54−z54
b
f(x,y,z)≈13−x108−y54−z54
c
f(x,y,z)≈13+x108+y54+z54
d
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108+y54+z54
e
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108−y108−z108
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4) is f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(2,4,4)=16. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fx(2,4,4)=−2(22+42+42)3/2=−1108,fy=−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fy(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154,fz=−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fz(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (2,4,4) is given by ∇f(2,4,4)=⟨fx(2,4,4),fy(2,4,4),fz(2,4,4)⟩=⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16+⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16−1108(x−2)−154(y−4)−154(z−4)=16−x108+154−y54+454−z54+454=13−x108−y54−z54.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2+z2. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4).

a
f(x,y,z)≈13−x54−y54−z54
b
f(x,y,z)≈13−x108−y54−z54
c
f(x,y,z)≈13+x108+y54+z54
d
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108+y54+z54
e
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108−y108−z108
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4) is f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(2,4,4)=16. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fx(2,4,4)=−2(22+42+42)3/2=−1108,fy=−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fy(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154,fz=−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fz(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (2,4,4) is given by ∇f(2,4,4)=⟨fx(2,4,4),fy(2,4,4),fz(2,4,4)⟩=⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16+⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16−1108(x−2)−154(y−4)−154(z−4)=16−x108+154−y54+454−z54+454=13−x108−y54−z54.

solution.reasoning: At (2,4,4), the radius is 6, so f=1/6 and ∇f=−(2,4,4)/6³=(−1/108,−1/54,−1/54). Thus L=1/6−(x−2)/108−(y−4)/54−(z−4)/54=1/3−x/108−y/54−z/54, matching option b. The mathematics is conclusive, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

feedback.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2+z2. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4).

a
f(x,y,z)≈13−x54−y54−z54
b
f(x,y,z)≈13−x108−y54−z54
c
f(x,y,z)≈13+x108+y54+z54
d
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108+y54+z54
e
f(x,y,z)≈−16−x108−y108−z108
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (2,4,4) is f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(2,4,4)=16. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=−x(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fx(2,4,4)=−2(22+42+42)3/2=−1108,fy=−y(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fy(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154,fz=−z(x2+y2+z2)3/2⇒fz(2,4,4)=−4(22+42+42)3/2=−154.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (2,4,4) is given by ∇f(2,4,4)=⟨fx(2,4,4),fy(2,4,4),fz(2,4,4)⟩=⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y,z)≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16+⟨−1108,−154,−154⟩⋅⟨x−2,y−4,z−4⟩=16−1108(x−2)−154(y−4)−154(z−4)=16−x108+154−y54+454−z54+454=13−x108−y54−z54.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,3)=-9,\,{f}_{x}(x,y,z)=y,\,{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=x,\,{f}_{z}(x,y,z)=-2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3),$ estimate the value of $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,3)+∇f(1,0,3)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,3),{f}_{y}(1,0,3),{f}_{z}(1,0,3)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-1.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y)=xy2−1. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3).

a
f(x,y)≈23−9x−6y
b
f(x,y)≈23+9x−6y
c
f(x,y)≈41+6x+12y
d
f(x,y)≈35+9x+12y
e
f(x,y)≈35−9x+6y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3) is f(x,y)≈f(−2,−3)+∇f(−2,−3)⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−2,−3)=−19. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=y2⇒fx(−2,−3)=(−3)2=9,fy=2xy⇒fy(−2,−3)=2(−2)(−3)=12.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−2,−3) is given by ∇f(−2,−3)=⟨9,12⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

last_observation.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Let f(x,y)=xy2−1. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3).

a
f(x,y)≈23−9x−6y
b
f(x,y)≈23+9x−6y
c
f(x,y)≈41+6x+12y
d
f(x,y)≈35+9x+12y
e
f(x,y)≈35−9x+6y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−2,−3) is f(x,y)≈f(−2,−3)+∇f(−2,−3)⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−2,−3)=−19. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=y2⇒fx(−2,−3)=(−3)2=9,fy=2xy⇒fy(−2,−3)=2(−2)(−3)=12.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−2,−3) is given by ∇f(−2,−3)=⟨9,12⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y)≈f(−2,−3)+∇f(−2,−3)⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩=−19+⟨9,12⟩⋅⟨x+2,y+3⟩=−19+9(x+2)+12(y+3)=35+9x+12y.

feedback.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-1.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Let f(x,y)=xey. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2).

a
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2−x−y
b
f(x,y)≈−2−x+y
c
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x−2y
d
f(x,y)≈−2+2x−2y
e
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x+y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−1,ln⁡2)=−2. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=ey⇒fx(−1,ln⁡2)=eln⁡2=2,fy=xey⇒fy(−1,ln⁡2)=−1eln⁡2=−2.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is given by ∇f(−1,ln⁡2)=⟨2,−2⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+⟨2,−2⟩⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+2(x+1)−2(y−ln⁡2)=2ln⁡2+2x−2y.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Let f(x,y)=xey. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2).

a
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2−x−y
b
f(x,y)≈−2−x+y
c
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x−2y
d
f(x,y)≈−2+2x−2y
e
f(x,y)≈2ln⁡2+2x+y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(−1,ln⁡2)=−2. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=ey⇒fx(−1,ln⁡2)=eln⁡2=2,fy=xey⇒fy(−1,ln⁡2)=−1eln⁡2=−2.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (−1,ln⁡2) is given by ∇f(−1,ln⁡2)=⟨2,−2⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is f(x,y)≈f(−1,ln⁡2)+∇f(−1,ln⁡2)⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+⟨2,−2⟩⋅⟨x+1,y−ln⁡2⟩=−2+2(x+1)−2(y−ln⁡2)=2ln⁡2+2x−2y.

solution.reasoning: At (−1, ln 2), f=−2, f_x=e^y=2, and f_y=xe^y=−2. Thus L(x,y)=−2+2(x+1)−2(y−ln 2)=2 ln 2+2x−2y, matching option c. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

feedback.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Suppose that f(x,y,z) is a differentiable function such that f(1,0,−1)=1,fx(1,0,−1)=−1,fy(1,0,−1)=−1,fz(1,0,−1)=0. Using a linear approximation of f at the point (1,0,−1) estimate the value of f(1.02,0.1,−0.96)

a
1.09
b
0.93
c
0.98
d
1.03
e
0.88
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (1,0,−1) is f(x,y,z)≈f(1,0,−1)+∇f(1,0,−1)⋅⟨x−1,y−0,z−(−1)⟩=f(1,0,−1)+⟨fx(1,0,−1),fy(1,0,−1),fz(1,0,−1)⟩⋅⟨x−1,y,z+1⟩=1+⟨−1,−1,0⟩⋅⟨x−1,y,z+1⟩.

We can approximate f(1.02,0.1,−0.96) by evaluating the linear approximation at x=1.02, y=0.1, and z=−0.96 as follows: f(1.02,0.1,−0.96)≈1+⟨−1,−1,0⟩⋅⟨1.02−1,0.1,−0.96+1⟩=1+⟨−1,−1,0⟩⋅⟨0.02,0.1,0.04⟩=1−1(0.02)−1(0.1)+0(0.04)=1−0.02−0.1+0=0.88

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we consider the expressions inside each of the parentheses. The first one is.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2} & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\times 25 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\times \frac{25}{1} & = \\ \frac{2\times 25}{5\times 1} & = \\ \frac{50}{5} & = \\ 10\end{aligned}
$$

The expression inside the second parentheses is.

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-2)}^{5}-(-20).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-2)}^{5}-(-20) & = \\ (-32)+20 & = \\ -12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{2}{5}\times {(-5)}^{2})÷({(-2)}^{5}-(-20)) & = \\ 10÷(-12) & = \\ \frac{10}{(-12)} & = \\ -\frac{10}{12} & = \\ -\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Evaluate $(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}).$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ 64\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64}{1}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64\times 3}{1\times 64} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{64}\times 3}{1\times \cancel{64}} & = \\ 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}) & = \\ (-3)\times 3 & = \\ -9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the value of $3+(-2+7)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

We begin by performing the operations inside the parentheses. So, first we add $(-2)$ to $7$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+(-2+7)^{2} & =3+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we compute the exponent:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+{5}^{2} & =3+25\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the numbers: 

$$
\begin{aligned}3+25=28\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Evaluate $(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}).$
question.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ 64\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64}{1}\times \frac{3}{64} & = \\ \frac{64\times 3}{1\times 64} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{64}\times 3}{1\times \cancel{64}} & = \\ 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\times ((-8)^{2}\times \frac{3}{64}) & = \\ (-3)\times 3 & = \\ -9\end{aligned}
$$
